profile.reading:
East Kentucky Network operates a data center at 271 Technology Trail in Ivel, Kentucky, a small unincorporated community in Floyd County in the state's eastern Appalachian coalfield region. East Kentucky Network was founded in 1991 and built its original business as a rural wireless carrier under the Appalachian Wireless brand, extending cellular service into mountainous parts of eastern Kentucky that larger national carriers had been slow to reach. Appalachian Wireless remains an active telecommunications brand for the company, and the Ivel data center appears to be a later extension of that same regional telecommunications infrastructure into enterprise data storage and colocation services.

On its own website, East Kentucky Network states the Ivel facility totals 16,700 square feet and includes redundant power sources and environmental controls intended to keep the site operating through utility outages and to maintain stable temperature and humidity for hosted equipment. The company also states that it maintains 100 gigabit per second connectivity from Ivel to major internet peering and colocation hubs in Chicago, Illinois, and Ashburn, Virginia, two of the most important interconnection points in the country, and that a similar link to Atlanta was planned as a further expansion at the time the company published its materials. East Kentucky Network describes its broader network as including a 400-mile redundant fiber loop and more than 7,500 combined fiber miles across its territory, infrastructure originally built to support wireless backhaul that a data center operator can also lease out or use to reach national interconnection points directly.

What the company's site does not publish is an IT power capacity in megawatts, a tier classification, industry compliance certifications, or the year the Ivel building itself was constructed or converted into a data center. For a rural eastern Kentucky facility built by a regional carrier rather than a national colocation brand, that gap is unsurprising. The site's real commercial value proposition rests less on published specifications and more on the fact that it offers a genuine national-grade fiber on-ramp from a part of the country where such infrastructure is otherwise scarce, a niche East Kentucky Network appears to be positioning the Ivel facility to fill for regional businesses, government agencies, and disaster-recovery customers seeking capacity outside major metro areas.

reading.body:
East Kentucky Network operates a 16,700 square foot data center in Ivel, Kentucky with redundant power and transport links to Chicago and Ashburn, but publishes no power capacity figures.

The facility's design reflects basic data center infrastructure priorities: redundancy for continuous operation and connectivity to major hub cities. These are the minimum requirements for any colocation or cloud service provider, not indicators of scale. The absence of a published megawatt rating means this facility's actual load on Kentucky's power grid cannot be determined from public sources.

This data captures physical footprint and stated capabilities but not power consumption. A 16,700 square foot building could draw anywhere from low single-digit megawatts to tens of megawatts depending on density, cooling approach, and utilization. The announced Atlanta hub remains future infrastructure, so its power implications are unknown. Without consumption data, the site's role in regional power demand cannot be assessed.
